Getting Started with datagoodr

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

What datagoodr is for

A CSV is just text. Whether 47401 is a ZIP code, a county FIPS, or a count is invisible to the file — so every program that opens it has to guess, and they guess differently. A leading zero disappears (06037 becomes 6037), a date is read in the wrong order, a column of codes is averaged as if it were a quantity. These small, silent errors are how ungoverned data quietly corrupts analysis.

datagoodr fixes this by pairing a dataset with a Data Governance File (DGF) — a small table, one row per variable, that records how each column is stored, how it should be read, and what it means. From that one artifact it produces a clean, self-describing dataset and a readable profile of it. It is built for the CSV world and meant to be edited in a spreadsheet, so governance does not require adopting a heavyweight platform. (For the bigger picture, see Rule-Based Data Governance.)

The three things datagoodr produces 

# datagoodr uses the formex package as its type-detection engine
remotes::install_github("lecy/formex")
remotes::install_github("UrbanInstitute/datagoodr")
library(datagoodr)

1. The DGF — a governed data dictionary. create_dgf() reads your data, profiles every column, and types it with the help of formex. The result is a table you can open in Excel and curate.

dgf <- create_dgf(raw_data, file = "DGF", open = FALSE)
# writes DGF.csv and DGF.xlsx, and returns the DGF data frame

2. A stabilized dataset — a governed CSV. stabilize_data() applies the DGF’s rules to a raw extract, producing a version that imports to the correct type where possible and safely (without data loss) where not — a date becomes ISO 2019-03-15, a ZIP keeps its leading zero.

stable <- stabilize_data(raw_data, dgf, use_v7 = TRUE)
write_stable_csv(stable, "data-governed.csv", dgf = dgf)

3. A Research Guide — a rendered data profile. create_rg() scaffolds a self-contained report that shows each variable with a visual tuned to its type (a histogram for a number, a treemap for a category, a calendar heat-map for a date).

create_rg(dgf, file = "research-guide")

The shape of the workflow 

raw CSV ──create_dgf()──▶ DGF ──┬── stabilize_data() ──▶ governed CSV
                 (profile + type)│
     you curate labels & types ──┘── create_rg() ───────▶ Research Guide

create_dgf() does the heavy first pass. Your job is to curate — add labels and definitions, confirm or correct the guessed types — in the spreadsheet. Then the same DGF drives both outputs, and update_dgf() re-profiles the data when it changes while keeping everything you curated.
